slides.narration: When a farmer is refused a land record, or a family quarrels over a house, or a person is held by the police without reason, where do they go for justice? In most cases, the answer lies within their own State: a district court or the High Court. In this chapter we study the High Court first, and then the courts of the district and the people's courts called Lok Adalats.

slides.heading: An integrated system of courts
slides.body_md: India has **one** connected judiciary: the **Supreme Court** at the top, a **High Court** for each State or group of States, and **subordinate courts** in every district.

slides.narration: Unlike some federal countries, India has one connected system of courts. The Supreme Court is at the top. Below it, each State, or group of States, has a High Court. Below the High Court are the district courts: the Court of the District Judge for civil cases and the Sessions Court for serious crimes, with smaller courts below them.

slides.heading: Composition of a High Court
slides.body_md: A Chief Justice and **as many other judges as the President decides**.

rows: As many as the President decides from time to time
For a temporary rise in work, up to 2 years
While a permanent judge is absent
Parliament may provide one for two or more States (Article 231)

visual.alt: Table of the composition of a High Court: a Chief Justice, other judges whose number the President fixes, additional judges for up to two years, acting judges during absence, and a common High Court for two or more States

slides.narration: Every High Court has a Chief Justice and other judges. The Constitution does not fix their number; the President decides it from time to time, so large States have bigger High Courts. Additional judges can be added for up to two years when work piles up, and acting judges can fill in during an absence. Parliament may also give two or more States a common High Court.

slides.heading: Quick check: a shared court
slides.body_md: Can two States share one High Court?
slides.narration: Some States in India share a High Court. Think about which body the Constitution allows to set this up.

slides.heading: Who can become a High Court judge?
slides.body_md: Citizenship plus **ten years** of the right experience.

rows: At least 10 years in a judicial office in India
At least 10 years as an advocate of a High Court

visual.alt: Table of qualifications of a High Court judge: Indian citizenship and either ten years of judicial office or ten years as a High Court advocate; retirement at sixty-two; no minimum age

slides.narration: To be appointed a High Court judge, a person must be a citizen of India and must have either held a judicial office in India for at least ten years or practised as an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years. Notice that no minimum age is fixed. A judge holds office until the age of sixty-two.

slides.heading: Appointment of judges
slides.body_md: The **President** appoints, after **consultation**.

nodes.label: Names recommended by a collegium of senior judges (practice since the 1990s)
Consultation: Chief Justice of India, Governor, Chief Justice of the High Court
Appointment by the President
Oath before the Governor

visual.alt: Flow of appointment of High Court judges: a collegium of senior judges recommends names, the President consults the Chief Justice of India, the Governor and the Chief Justice of the High Court, then appoints; the judge takes oath before the Governor
visual.caption: Article 217.

slides.narration: Judges of a High Court are appointed by the President. Before appointing them, the President consults the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State and, for ordinary judges, the Chief Justice of that High Court. In practice, since the nineteen nineties, names are recommended by a collegium of senior judges. A new judge takes the oath before the Governor.

slides.heading: Quick check: retirement
slides.body_md: Up to what age does a High Court judge serve?
slides.narration: The retirement ages of Supreme Court and High Court judges are different. Which one applies here?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: who acts?
slides.body_md: Four imagined situations: who takes the decision?
bullets: Appointment and transfer: the **President**, after consultation.
Removal: **Parliament** by special majority, then the **President**.
Retirement: automatic at **62**.

rows: A judge is moved to another State
The President, after consulting the Chief Justice of India
A judge is accused of proved misbehaviour

visual.alt: Worked example table: a new judge is appointed by the President after consultation; a transfer is ordered by the President after consulting the Chief Justice of India; removal needs a special majority in Parliament and then the President; at sixty-two a judge retires

slides.narration: Let us test ourselves. When a new judge is needed, the President appoints after consultation. To move a judge to another High Court, the President acts after consulting the Chief Justice of India. If a judge is accused of proved misbehaviour, both Houses of Parliament must pass an address by a special majority before the President removes him. At sixty-two a judge simply retires.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting a special majority
slides.body_md: Both conditions must be met in **each** House.

visual.alt: Worked example table for removal: in a Lok Sabha of 543, a majority of the total membership is 272; if 480 members vote, two-thirds is 320; both conditions are met with 320 votes in favour
visual.caption: Imagined attendance; both conditions must be met.

slides.narration: Removal needs a special majority. In each House, the address must be supported by a majority of the total membership and by two-thirds of the members present and voting. In a Lok Sabha of five hundred and forty-three, the first condition needs two hundred and seventy-two. If four hundred and eighty vote, two-thirds is three hundred and twenty, so three hundred and twenty votes meet both conditions.

slides.heading: Keeping judges independent

nodes.label: Appointment by the President, with judicial consultation
Tenure till 62; removal only by Parliament and the President
Salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State
No practice before the same High Court after retirement

visual.alt: Flow of safeguards of independence: appointment by the President with judicial consultation, tenure till sixty-two with difficult removal, salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State, and no practice before the same High Court after retirement
visual.caption: Why judges can decide without fear.

slides.narration: Why can judges decide cases against powerful governments? Several safeguards help. They are appointed by the President, not by the State government. They serve till sixty-two and can be removed only through Parliament. Their salaries come from the Consolidated Fund of the State and cannot be cut during their term. And after retiring, they cannot practise before the same High Court.

slides.heading: Original jurisdiction
slides.body_md: Cases the High Court hears **for the first time**.

rows: Fundamental Rights and other legal rights
Disputes over elections to Parliament or the State Legislature
Some civil matters (in some High Courts)
Certain admiralty, company or matrimonial cases

visual.alt: Table of original jurisdiction of a High Court: writs under Article 226, election petitions for Parliament and the State Legislature, and in some High Courts certain civil matters

slides.narration: Original jurisdiction means hearing a case at its very start. A High Court hears writ petitions under Article two hundred and twenty-six, and petitions challenging elections to Parliament and the State Legislature. Some High Courts also hear certain civil matters directly, such as admiralty or company cases. For most ordinary disputes, however, the case begins in a lower court.

slides.heading: The five writs

rows: A public authority fails in its duty
A lower court goes beyond its powers in a pending case
A lower court's order is quashed after decision
A person holds a public office without right

visual.alt: Table of the five writs with their literal ideas and uses: habeas corpus for unlawful detention, mandamus for a duty not done, prohibition to stop a lower court in a pending case, certiorari to quash a decided order, quo warranto to test a right to public office

slides.narration: A writ is a formal order of a court. Habeas corpus asks for a detained person to be produced. Mandamus commands an official to do a duty. Prohibition stops a lower court from going beyond its powers in a pending case. Certiorari quashes a lower court's order after it is made. Quo warranto asks a person by what authority he holds a public office.

slides.heading: Why the High Court's writ power is wider
slides.body_md: Article 226 covers Fundamental Rights **and any other purpose**.

rows: Fundamental Rights and any other purpose

visual.alt: Table comparing writ powers: a High Court acts for Fundamental Rights and any other purpose within its territory, at its discretion; the Supreme Court acts only for Fundamental Rights across India, and the right to approach it is itself fundamental

slides.narration: Both the Supreme Court and the High Courts issue the same five writs, but the High Court's power is wider in one way. Under Article two hundred and twenty-six, it can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose, such as an ordinary legal right. The Supreme Court, under Article thirty-two, issues writs only for Fundamental Rights, though across the whole country.

slides.heading: Quick check: supervising tribunals
slides.body_md: Which Article gives the High Court superintendence over courts and tribunals?
slides.narration: A High Court watches over every court and tribunal in its State, except military tribunals. Which Article gives it this power?

slides.heading: Appellate jurisdiction
slides.body_md: Appeals in **civil** and **criminal** cases.

nodes.label: Lower civil courts
Court of the District Judge
High Court (civil appeals)
Supreme Court

visual.alt: Flow of civil appeals: lower civil courts, the Court of the District Judge, the High Court and finally the Supreme Court
visual.caption: Civil chain of appeal.

slides.narration: Most cases reach a High Court on appeal. In civil cases, appeals come from the Court of the District Judge and other civil courts. In criminal cases, appeals come from the Sessions Court, and a death sentence passed by a Sessions Court cannot be carried out until the High Court confirms it. From the High Court, a further appeal may lie to the Supreme Court.

slides.heading: Revision and superintendence

rows: Call for the record of a decided case where no appeal lies and correct errors of jurisdiction
Supervise all courts and tribunals in its territory, except military tribunals
Take up a case raising a substantial question of constitutional law

visual.alt: Table of supervisory powers: revisory power over decided cases where no appeal lies, superintendence over all courts and tribunals under Article 227, and transfer of cases raising constitutional questions

slides.narration: Even where no appeal is allowed, a High Court can call for the record of a case decided by a lower court and correct it if that court acted without power or with serious irregularity. This is its revisory jurisdiction. Under Article two hundred and twenty-seven, it also supervises all courts and tribunals in its territory, except military tribunals.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: which jurisdiction?
slides.body_md: Match four imagined cases to the power used.

rows: A losing candidate challenges a State election
An appeal against a District Judge's civil decree
A lower court decided a case it had no power to hear; no appeal lies
A State law is challenged as against Fundamental Rights

visual.alt: Worked example table matching imagined cases to jurisdiction: an election challenge is original, an appeal from a District Judge is appellate, correcting a lower court that lacked power is revisory, and testing a State law is judicial review

slides.narration: Try these four. A losing candidate challenging a State election goes straight to the High Court, so that is original jurisdiction. An appeal against a District Judge's decree is appellate. Correcting a lower court that heard a case it had no power to hear, where no appeal lies, is revisory. Striking down a State law that violates Fundamental Rights is judicial review.

slides.heading: Court of Record and judicial review

rows: Laws and executive orders tested against the Constitution
Cited as precedents; bind lower courts
Power to punish for contempt of itself
Protects Fundamental Rights and the federal balance

visual.alt: Two-column table: as a Court of Record a High Court preserves its judgements, which bind lower courts and are cited as precedents, and can punish contempt; through judicial review it tests laws and orders and declares unconstitutional ones void

slides.narration: Under Article two hundred and fifteen, every High Court is a Court of Record. Its judgements are preserved, bind the courts below and are cited as precedents, and it can punish anyone for contempt of itself. Through judicial review, a High Court can test any law or executive order against the Constitution and declare it void if it violates the Constitution.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: A Chief Justice and other judges; the President fixes the number; common High Courts are possible.
Citizen with ten years of judicial office or High Court practice; retires at 62.
Appointed by the President after consultation; removed only through a special majority in Parliament.
Original (writs, election petitions), appellate, revisory and supervisory powers; Court of Record; judicial review.

nodes.label: Chief Justice and other judges fixed by the President
Citizen with ten years of judicial office or High Court practice
Appointed by the President; removed only through Parliament
Original, appellate, revisory, writ and review powers; Court of Record

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: composition, qualifications, appointment and removal, and the jurisdiction of a High Court
visual.caption: Part 1 in four lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. A High Court has a Chief Justice and other judges whose number the President fixes. Judges must be citizens with ten years of judicial office or High Court practice, and they retire at sixty-two. The President appoints them after consultation, and only Parliament can begin their removal. The High Court has original, appellate, revisory and writ powers, and is a Court of Record.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: No minimum age for a High Court judge; retirement at **62** (Supreme Court: 65).
The **President** appoints; the Governor is only **consulted**.
Article **226** is wider than Article **32**: "any other purpose".
High Courts have **no advisory** jurisdiction.
10-mark answers: one clear point per mark in each part.
slides.narration: A few tips. Do not invent a minimum age for High Court judges, and remember they retire at sixty-two. The President appoints them; the Governor is only consulted. When comparing writ powers, mention that Article two hundred and twenty-six covers any other purpose. Never say a High Court gives advisory opinions. And in long answers, give one point for every mark.

slides.narration: Most citizens never see the inside of the Supreme Court. Their disputes begin and usually end in their own district. In Part 2 we visit the district court complex: the Court of the District Judge for civil matters, the Sessions Court for serious crimes, and the Lok Adalat, where neighbours can settle a quarrel by agreement without paying any court fee.

slides.narration: Look again at the hierarchy. Below the High Court, each district has two main branches. On the civil side, the Court of the District Judge sits above the lower civil courts. On the criminal side, the Sessions Court sits above the magistrates' courts. Both are supervised by the High Court, which also hears appeals from them.

slides.heading: The Court of the District Judge

rows: The Governor, in consultation with the High Court (Article 233)
At least 7 years as an advocate
Civil appeals from lower courts; important civil suits; supervision of civil courts

visual.alt: Table on the Court of the District Judge: appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court; seven years as an advocate for direct appointment; hears civil appeals, important civil suits and supervises lower civil courts

slides.narration: The Court of the District Judge is the highest civil court of a district. District Judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court. A lawyer can be appointed directly after at least seven years of practice. The court hears appeals from lower civil courts, tries important civil suits about property, contracts and succession, and supervises the civil courts of the district.

slides.heading: Quick check: from the Bar
slides.body_md: How many years of practice are needed for direct appointment as a District Judge?
slides.narration: The experience needed for a District Judge is different from that for a High Court judge. How many years of practice are needed?

slides.heading: The Sessions Court

rows: Serious crimes such as murder, robbery and dacoity
Any lawful sentence; a death sentence needs High Court confirmation
From judgements of magistrates' courts in the district

visual.alt: Table on the Sessions Court: tries serious crimes such as murder, robbery and dacoity, can pass any lawful sentence with death sentences confirmed by the High Court, and hears appeals from magistrates

slides.narration: The Sessions Court tries serious crimes such as murder, robbery and dacoity. It can pass any sentence the law allows, but a death sentence cannot be carried out unless the High Court confirms it. The Sessions Court also hears appeals against judgements of the magistrates' courts in the district.

slides.heading: One officer, two titles
slides.body_md: District Judge for **civil** work; Sessions Judge for **criminal** work.

visual.alt: Comparison table: the District Judge hears civil cases such as property and contract disputes and civil appeals; the Sessions Judge hears criminal cases such as murder and criminal appeals from magistrates; both are appealed to the High Court

slides.narration: In most districts, the same senior judicial officer heads both branches. When he hears a dispute about property or a contract, he sits as the District Judge. When he tries a murder case, he sits as the Sessions Judge. Appeals from both branches go to the High Court.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: tracing a criminal case
slides.body_md: An imagined theft case climbs the ladder.

nodes.label: Theft case: Judicial Magistrate
Appeal: Sessions Court
Further appeal or revision: High Court
Supreme Court (only on serious points)

visual.alt: Worked example flow of an imagined theft case: tried by a Judicial Magistrate, appealed to the Sessions Court, then to the High Court, and to the Supreme Court only on serious points
visual.caption: Trace the route, court by court.

slides.narration: Follow an imagined theft case. It is first tried by a Judicial Magistrate. If the convict is unhappy, he appeals to the Sessions Court. From there he may go to the High Court, by appeal or revision. Only on serious points of law or fact does the matter reach the Supreme Court. Each step up is a chance to correct mistakes.

slides.heading: Quick check: civil or criminal?

sections.heading: 2. Qualifications, appointment, transfer and removal
sections.body_md:
- **Qualifications:** citizen of India; **ten years** in a judicial office in India **or** ten years as an advocate of a High Court. No minimum age; retirement at **62**.
- **Appointment:** by the **President** after consulting the **Chief Justice of India**, the **Governor** and the **Chief Justice of the High Court**; in practice names come from a **collegium** of senior judges (since the 1990s). Oath before the Governor.
- **Transfer:** by the President after consulting the Chief Justice of India (Article 222).
- **Removal:** as for a Supreme Court judge: an address by **each House of Parliament** supported by a **majority of its total membership** and **two-thirds of those present and voting**, on proved **misbehaviour or incapacity**; order by the President.

sections.heading: 3. Independence of High Court judges
sections.body_md:
- Appointment by the **President** with judicial consultation, not by the State government.
- **Security of tenure** till 62; removal only through **Parliament**.
- **Salaries** charged on the **Consolidated Fund of the State**; cannot be reduced during the term except in a financial emergency.
- A retired permanent judge **may not plead** before the same High Court (only the Supreme Court and other High Courts).

sections.heading: 4. Jurisdiction and writs
sections.body_md:
- **Original:** writs under **Article 226**; **election petitions** for Parliament and the State Legislature; in some High Courts certain civil matters.
- **Writs:** habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto. Article 226 covers Fundamental Rights **and any other purpose** (wider than Article 32, which covers Fundamental Rights only; Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right).
- **Appellate:** civil appeals from the District Judge and other civil courts; criminal appeals from the Sessions Court; **confirmation of death sentences**.
- **Revisory and supervisory:** revision of decided cases where no appeal lies; **superintendence** over all courts and tribunals (except military) under **Article 227**.
- **Judicial review:** laws and executive orders declared void if unconstitutional.
- **Court of Record (Article 215):** judgements preserved and cited as precedents; binding on lower courts; power to punish for contempt.
- **No advisory** jurisdiction.

sections.heading: 5. Subordinate courts: District Judge and Sessions Court
sections.body_md:
- **District Judge:** appointed by the **Governor in consultation with the High Court** (**Article 233**); direct appointment from the Bar needs **seven years** as an advocate. Hears **civil appeals** from lower courts, tries important **civil suits**, supervises civil courts.
- **Sessions Court:** tries **serious crimes** (murder, robbery, dacoity); hears appeals from **magistrates**; can pass any lawful sentence, but a **death sentence** must be **confirmed by the High Court** (criminal procedure law; the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure from 1 July 2024 and keeps this rule).
- The same officer is usually the **District Judge** for civil work and the **Sessions Judge** for criminal work.

sections.heading: 6. Lok Adalats
sections.body_md:
- **Meaning:** a **people's court** that settles disputes by **compromise**. Lok Adalats began in the early 1980s and were given statutory status by the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.
- **Working:** a bench, usually a serving or retired **judicial officer** with a lawyer or social worker; cases **pending** in courts or at the **pre-litigation** stage; mainly civil and compoundable matters.
- **Status of awards:** **deemed decree of a civil court**; **final and binding**; **no appeal**.
- **Advantages:** no court fee (fee refunded on settlement of a pending case); speed; informality; finality; goodwill; reduces backlog.
- **Limits:** needs consent of both sides; not for serious non-compoundable crimes.

questions.stem_md: Who decides how many judges, besides the Chief Justice, a High Court will have?

options.text_md: The Governor of the State
The President of India
The State Legislative Assembly
The Chief Minister of the State

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The President of India. The Constitution gives each High Court a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President thinks necessary from time to time; there is no fixed number. The Governor, the Assembly and the Chief Minister do not fix the strength.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined neighbouring States, Pashmir and Tarai, share a single High Court. Is this allowed?

options.text_md: No; every State must have its own High Court
Only if both States are Union Territories
Only for criminal cases; civil cases need separate High Courts
Yes; Parliament may set up a common High Court for two or more States or Union Territories

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Yes; Parliament may set up a common High Court for two or more States or Union Territories. Article 231 allows Parliament to establish one High Court for two or more States, or for States and a Union Territory. Several such common High Courts exist. The other options add conditions the Constitution does not lay down.

questions.stem_md: Advocate Farida Qureshi (imagined) has practised before a High Court for eleven years. Which further condition must she meet to be eligible for appointment as a High Court judge?

options.text_md: She must be a citizen of India
She must be at least 45 years old
She must have served as a District Judge
She must be a member of the State Bar Council for 20 years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** She must be a citizen of India. A High Court judge must be an Indian citizen who has either held a judicial office in India for ten years or been a High Court advocate for ten years. She already has eleven years at the Bar, so citizenship is the remaining condition. No minimum age is laid down, and service as a District Judge is an alternative route, not a requirement.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is one of the two alternative routes of experience that make a citizen eligible to be appointed a High Court judge?

options.text_md: At least five years as a member of a State Legislative Assembly
At least ten years as a professor of law
At least ten years in a judicial office in India
At least seven years as a Supreme Court advocate only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** At least ten years in a judicial office in India. The two routes are ten years in a judicial office in India, or ten years as an advocate of a High Court (or of two or more High Courts in succession). Legislative service is irrelevant, and a law professor is not eligible on that ground alone for a High Court post.

questions.stem_md: Who formally appoints the judges of a High Court?

options.text_md: The Governor of the State
The Chief Justice of India
The President of India
The Union Law Minister

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The President of India. High Court judges are appointed by the President, after consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the State (and, for judges other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of that High Court). The Governor is consulted but does not appoint.

questions.stem_md: Up to what age does a permanent judge of a High Court hold office?

options.text_md: 62 years
65 years
60 years
70 years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 62 years. A High Court judge holds office until the age of 62. Sixty-five is the retirement age of Supreme Court judges; the other figures do not apply.

questions.stem_md: A High Court judge in an imagined State is accused of proved misbehaviour. Which authority alone can finally remove him from office?

options.text_md: The Governor, on the advice of the State Council of Ministers
The Chief Justice of India, acting alone
The State Legislative Assembly, by a simple majority
The President, after both Houses of Parliament pass an address by a special majority

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The President, after both Houses of Parliament pass an address by a special majority. A High Court judge is removed in the same way as a Supreme Court judge: the President issues the order after each House of Parliament passes an address supported by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. The State government and Assembly have no power of removal.

questions.stem_md: A judge of one High Court is moved to the High Court of another State. Under the Constitution, who orders such a transfer?

options.text_md: The Governor of the new State
The President, after consulting the Chief Justice of India
The Chief Justice of the old High Court alone
Parliament, by passing a law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The President, after consulting the Chief Justice of India. Article 222 allows the President, after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, to transfer a judge from one High Court to another. The Governor and the Chief Justice of the High Court do not order transfers, and no separate law is needed for each case.

Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both statements are true, and R explains A. The bar on practising before the court where one served (a retired judge may plead only before the Supreme Court and other High Courts) keeps the judiciary free of suspicion and so supports its independence.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Constitution fixes a minimum age of 35 years for appointment as a High Court judge.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** No minimum age is fixed for a High Court judge; the conditions are citizenship and ten years of judicial office or of practice as a High Court advocate. Thirty-five is the age for the President and Vice-President.

questions.stem_md: A permanent judge of a High Court holds office until the age of ___ years.
questions.solution_md: The retirement age of a High Court judge is 62 years.

questions.stem_md: State the qualifications a person needs to be appointed a judge of a High Court.
questions.solution_md: Citizenship plus either of the two ten-year routes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The person must be a **citizen of India**.
2. The person must have held a **judicial office in India for at least ten years**, **or** have been an **advocate of a High Court for at least ten years**.

marking_scheme.step: Ten years of judicial office or of High Court practice

questions.stem_md: Whom does the President consult before appointing a judge (other than the Chief Justice) to a High Court?
questions.solution_md: Three consultees; collegium practice optional.

answer.model_answer_md: The President consults the **Chief Justice of India**, the **Governor of the State** and the **Chief Justice of that High Court**. In practice, since the 1990s the names come from a **collegium of senior judges**.

marking_scheme.step: Chief Justice of India and Governor
Chief Justice of the High Court (or the collegium practice)

questions.stem_md: An imagined High Court has a sudden pile-up of pending appeals. What kind of judge can the President appoint to deal with it, and for how long?
questions.solution_md: Additional judges, two years.

answer.model_answer_md: The President may appoint **additional judges** to clear a temporary increase in work or arrears, for a period of **up to two years**. (An **acting judge** may also be appointed when a permanent judge is absent.)

questions.stem_md: Explain three provisions that keep the judges of a High Court independent of the State government.
questions.solution_md: Any three independence safeguards with a line of explanation each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Security of tenure:** a judge serves till 62 and can be removed only by the **President** after a **special majority in Parliament**, not by the State government.
2. **Salaries** are charged on the **Consolidated Fund of the State** and cannot be reduced during the term (except in a financial emergency).
3. A retired judge **cannot practise before the same High Court**, so judges have no reason to please future litigants.

marking_scheme.step: Security of tenure and removal procedure
Bar on practice (or another valid safeguard)

questions.stem_md:
An imagined State, Varunpradesh, has just been formed and needs a High Court.

(i) Describe the composition of a High Court and state whether Varunpradesh could share a High Court with a neighbour. **[3]**
(ii) State the qualifications for appointment as a judge of the new High Court. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how its judges are appointed, transferred and removed. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Composition and common court; qualifications; appointment, transfer and removal.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A High Court has a **Chief Justice** and **such other judges as the President** decides from time to time; **additional** and **acting** judges may also be appointed. Under **Article 231**, Parliament may set up a **common High Court** for two or more States, so Varunpradesh **could share** one.

(ii) A judge must be a **citizen of India** and must have held a **judicial office for ten years** or been an **advocate of a High Court for ten years**. No minimum age is fixed; judges retire at **62**.

(iii) The **President** appoints the judges after consulting the **Chief Justice of India**, the **Governor** and the **Chief Justice of the High Court**; in practice a **collegium** of senior judges recommends names. The President may **transfer** a judge to another High Court after consulting the Chief Justice of India. A judge is **removed** by the President only after **each House of Parliament** passes an address by a **special majority** on grounds of proved **misbehaviour or incapacity**.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Chief Justice and other judges fixed by the President
(ii) Ten years of judicial office or practice
(iii) Appointment by the President after consultation
(iii) Transfer and removal by special majority

questions.stem_md:
A student debate in an imagined school asks whether High Court judges are truly free from pressure.

(i) Explain how the method of appointment helps keep the judges independent. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the security of tenure and the removal procedure protect them. **[3]**
(iii) Give two other safeguards of independence and evaluate whether, together, they are enough. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Appointment; tenure and removal; two further safeguards plus a balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Judges are appointed by the **President**, not by the State government, after consulting the **Chief Justice of India** and senior judges; the **collegium** practice gives judges themselves the main voice, so appointments do not depend on **party politics**.

(ii) A judge holds office **till 62** and can be removed only by the **President** after **both Houses of Parliament** pass an address by a **special majority** for proved **misbehaviour or incapacity**. Because this is so difficult, a judge can decide cases **without fear** of losing the post.

(iii) **Salaries** are charged on the **Consolidated Fund** and cannot be cut during the term (except in a financial emergency), and a retired judge **cannot practise** before the same High Court. Together these give strong protection; a fair view is that independence also depends on **timely appointments** and on judges' own **integrity**, which no rule can fully guarantee.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Appointment by the President with judicial consultation

questions.stem_md: Why is the writ jurisdiction of a High Court described as wider than that of the Supreme Court?

options.text_md: A High Court can issue writs to enforce Fundamental Rights and also for any other purpose, such as an ordinary legal right
A High Court can issue writs against the President, which the Supreme Court cannot
A High Court can issue more than five kinds of writs
A High Court's writs apply across the whole of India, while the Supreme Court's apply to one State

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A High Court can issue writs to enforce Fundamental Rights and also for any other purpose, such as an ordinary legal right. Under Article 226 a High Court may issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and "for any other purpose", while Article 32 lets the Supreme Court issue writs only for Fundamental Rights. Both use the same five writs, and a High Court's writs run only within its own territory.

questions.stem_md: Rohan Bhatia (imagined) lost a Lok Sabha election by a few votes and believes the counting was unlawful. Where must he file his election petition at first instance?

options.text_md: In the Supreme Court directly
In the High Court of the State
In the Court of the District Judge
Before a Lok Adalat

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** In the High Court of the State. Disputes about elections to Parliament and the State Legislature are tried by the High Court in its original jurisdiction; an appeal then lies to the Supreme Court. District courts and Lok Adalats do not hear election petitions.

questions.stem_md: A trader is unhappy with the decision of the Court of the District Judge in a civil dispute over a warehouse. To which court does his appeal normally lie?

options.text_md: The Sessions Court
A Lok Adalat
The High Court of the State
The Court of a Judicial Magistrate

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The High Court of the State. Appeals in civil cases from the District Judge lie to the High Court under its appellate jurisdiction. The Sessions Court hears criminal cases; a Lok Adalat settles disputes by agreement and is not an appeal court; a magistrate is lower in rank.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following follows from a High Court being a Court of Record?

options.text_md: It can hear cases only after they have been recorded in a Lok Adalat
It keeps a record of all elections held in the State
It can record evidence only in civil cases
Its judgements are preserved and can be cited as precedents, and it can punish for contempt of itself

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Its judgements are preserved and can be cited as precedents, and it can punish for contempt of itself. Article 215 makes every High Court a Court of Record: its decisions are kept as records with evidentiary value, are binding on courts below and are cited as precedents, and it has the power to punish for contempt of itself. The other options describe nothing of the kind.

questions.stem_md: A High Court finds that a tribunal in its State has been ignoring its own procedure rules. Under which Article can it exercise superintendence over that tribunal?

options.text_md: Article 32
Article 123
Article 72
Article 227

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Article 227. Article 227 gives every High Court superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory (except military tribunals). Article 32 concerns Supreme Court writs, Article 123 ordinances and Article 72 the President's mercy powers.

questions.stem_md: A lower court in an imagined district decided a small case although the law did not give it power over such cases, and no appeal is allowed. How can the High Court step in?

options.text_md: By referring the case to the Governor for a pardon
By transferring the judge to another State
By calling for the record and revising the decision under its revisory jurisdiction
It cannot step in because no appeal lies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** By calling for the record and revising the decision under its revisory jurisdiction. Even where no appeal lies, a High Court can call for the record of a case decided by a subordinate court and correct it if that court acted without jurisdiction or with serious irregularity. Pardons and transfers have nothing to do with correcting a decision.

questions.stem_md: An imagined State passes a law that takes away a citizen's right to move freely between districts. A High Court strikes it down. Which power has the High Court used?

options.text_md: Advisory jurisdiction
Judicial review
Original jurisdiction in election petitions
Power of pardon

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Judicial review. Judicial review is the power to examine laws and executive orders and declare them void if they violate the Constitution, here a Fundamental Right. High Courts have no advisory jurisdiction; election petitions and pardons are unrelated.

questions.stem_md: Sunaina's brother has been held by the police for days without being produced before a magistrate. Which writ should she ask the High Court for?

options.text_md: Habeas corpus
Quo warranto
Certiorari
Mandamus

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Habeas corpus. Habeas corpus orders the person holding someone in custody to produce him before the court, so the court can decide whether the detention is lawful. Quo warranto questions a person's right to hold a public office; certiorari quashes a lower court's order; mandamus orders a public official to perform a duty.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A citizen whose ordinary legal right (not a Fundamental Right) is violated by a State authority can seek a writ from the High Court.

**Reason (R):** The right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights is itself a Fundamental Right.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. A is true because Article 226 lets a High Court issue writs "for any other purpose". R describes Article 32, which concerns the Supreme Court and Fundamental Rights only, so it is not the reason for A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A High Court can punish a person for contempt of itself.

**Reason (R):** A High Court gets its power to punish for contempt from an order of the State Governor.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true; R is false. The power comes from the Constitution: Article 215 makes the High Court a Court of Record with all its powers, including the power to punish for contempt of itself. The Governor confers no such power.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Like the Supreme Court, a High Court can give advisory opinions to the Governor on questions of law.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** High Courts have no advisory jurisdiction. Only the Supreme Court can advise, and only when the President refers a question under Article 143.

questions.stem_md: Article 215 declares every High Court to be a Court of ___.
questions.solution_md: Every High Court is a Court of Record under Article 215.

questions.stem_md: Match each writ that a High Court can issue with what it does.

options.text_md: Habeas corpus
Mandamus
Prohibition
Quo warranto

match_right.text_md: Orders a public authority to perform a legal duty
Asks a person by what right he holds a public office
Orders a detained person to be produced before the court
Stops a lower court from going beyond its powers in a pending case

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Habeas corpus: produce the body. Mandamus: perform your duty. Prohibition: stop proceeding beyond jurisdiction (issued while the case is pending; certiorari quashes after the decision). Quo warranto: show your authority to hold the office.

questions.stem_md: Give two kinds of matters that a High Court can hear directly in its original jurisdiction.
questions.solution_md: Any two valid original matters.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Writ petitions** for the enforcement of **Fundamental Rights** and other legal rights (**Article 226**).
2. **Election petitions** challenging elections to **Parliament** or the **State Legislature**. (Some High Courts also hear certain civil matters, such as admiralty or company cases, at first instance.)

questions.stem_md: Explain the appellate jurisdiction of a High Court in civil and in criminal cases.
questions.solution_md: One line each for civil and criminal appeals.

answer.model_answer_md: **Civil:** the High Court hears appeals against decisions of the **Court of the District Judge** and other subordinate civil courts. **Criminal:** it hears appeals against convictions by the **Sessions Court**, and a **death sentence** passed by a Sessions Court must be **confirmed** by it.

marking_scheme.step: Criminal appeals (and confirmation of death sentences)

questions.stem_md: State two consequences of a High Court being a Court of Record.
questions.solution_md: Records and precedents; contempt power.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Its **judgements are preserved** and can be **cited as precedents**; they bind the **courts below** it.
2. It has the power to **punish for contempt** of itself.

questions.stem_md: How does a High Court supervise the courts below it? Give two ways.
questions.solution_md: Any two supervisory powers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Under **Article 227** it has **superintendence** over all courts and tribunals in its territory.
2. It can **revise** their decided cases, take up cases raising a **constitutional question**, and is consulted on appointing **district judges**.

questions.stem_md: Compare the writ jurisdiction of a High Court with that of the Supreme Court on three points.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct points of comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Purpose:** a High Court (Article 226) issues writs for Fundamental Rights **and for any other purpose**; the Supreme Court (Article 32) only for **Fundamental Rights**.
2. **Area:** a High Court's writs run within **its territory**; the Supreme Court's run throughout **India**.
3. **Nature:** Article 32 is itself a **Fundamental Right**, so the Supreme Court cannot refuse to act on a proper petition; a High Court's writ power is **discretionary**.

questions.stem_md:
Read the situation and answer. *(Imagined.)* A law student is preparing a chart of the powers of the High Court of her State.

(i) Explain the original jurisdiction of a High Court with two examples. **[3]**
(ii) Explain its appellate jurisdiction in civil and criminal cases. **[3]**
(iii) Explain its revisory jurisdiction and its position as a Court of Record. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Original; appellate; revisory and Court of Record.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Original jurisdiction** means hearing a case **for the first time**. A High Court hears **writ petitions** under **Article 226** for Fundamental Rights and other legal rights, and **election petitions** about elections to Parliament and the State Legislature; some High Courts also hear certain **civil** matters directly.

(ii) In **civil** cases it hears **appeals** against decisions of the **District Judge** and other subordinate civil courts. In **criminal** cases it hears appeals against **Sessions Court** convictions, and a **death sentence** passed by a Sessions Court needs its **confirmation**.

(iii) Under its **revisory** power it can **call for the record** of a case decided by a lower court where **no appeal lies** and correct it if that court acted **without jurisdiction** or with serious **irregularity**; under **Article 227** it supervises all courts and tribunals in its territory. As a **Court of Record** (**Article 215**) its judgements are **preserved**, **bind lower courts** and are **cited as precedents**, and it can **punish for contempt** of itself.

questions.stem_md:
Three imagined citizens of Varunpradesh approach the High Court.

- Meher has been detained by the police for a week without being produced before a magistrate.
- A municipal board refuses to issue Arvind's trade licence although he meets every condition.
- A man appointed as head of a State corporation does not have the qualifications the law requires.

(i) Name the writ each person should seek and say why. **[3]**
(ii) Under which Article does the High Court issue writs, and why is this power called wider than the Supreme Court's? **[3]**
(iii) Explain judicial review by a High Court and why it matters for citizens. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Three writs with reasons; Article 226 and its width; judicial review and why it matters.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Meher: **habeas corpus**, so that the court can examine whether her **detention** is lawful. Arvind: **mandamus**, ordering the board to **perform its legal duty**. The corporation case: **quo warranto**, asking the man **by what authority** he holds the office.

(ii) **Article 226**. It is wider because a High Court can issue writs not only for **Fundamental Rights** but also **for any other purpose**, such as ordinary legal rights, whereas under **Article 32** the Supreme Court issues writs only for Fundamental Rights.

(iii) **Judicial review** is the power to examine **laws** and **executive actions** and declare them **void** if they **violate the Constitution**. It matters because it protects **Fundamental Rights**, keeps the Union and State governments within their **constitutional limits**, and gives citizens a **nearby court** to challenge unlawful action.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Any other purpose versus Fundamental Rights only

questions.stem_md: Read the extract from the imagined diary of a law intern at a High Court and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people and places in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** An order to a public authority to do its duty.

**(b)** Appeals from the Sessions Court.

**(c) (i)** Court of Record; one further consequence.

**OR (c) (ii)** Width of Article 226.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Mandamus**, ordering the officer to perform his legal duty.

**(b)** Its **appellate jurisdiction** in **criminal** cases (including confirming a death sentence).

**(c) (i)** It is a **Court of Record** (Article 215), so it can **punish for contempt** of itself; its **judgements are preserved** and **cited as precedents**.

**OR (c) (ii)** Under **Article 226** a High Court can issue writs **for any other purpose**, not only for **Fundamental Rights**, so an ordinary legal right is also protected.

questions.passage_md:
**Diary of a law intern (imagined)**

Monday. First case of the morning: a farmer from a hill district whose land records a revenue officer refused to correct, though the law requires it. His lawyer asked the High Court to order the officer to act. The judge agreed.

Wednesday. A bench heard an appeal against a Sessions Court that had convicted three men of robbery. Later, the same bench was asked to confirm a death sentence passed by another Sessions Court.

Friday. A shopkeeper who had insulted the court in a newspaper was called to explain why he should not be punished for contempt.

children.stem_md: Which writ did the farmer obtain on Monday?
children.solution_md: An order to a public authority to do its duty.

answer.model_answer_md: **Mandamus**, ordering the officer to perform his legal duty.

children.stem_md: Which jurisdiction was the High Court using on Wednesday?

answer.model_answer_md: Its **appellate jurisdiction** in **criminal** cases (including confirming a death sentence).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Which status of the High Court allowed it to act on Friday? State one other consequence of that status.
children.solution_md: Court of Record; one further consequence.

answer.model_answer_md: It is a **Court of Record** (Article 215), so it can **punish for contempt** of itself; its **judgements are preserved** and **cited as precedents**.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): The farmer's right was an ordinary legal right, not a Fundamental Right. Explain why he could still go to the High Court for a writ.

answer.model_answer_md: Under **Article 226** a High Court can issue writs **for any other purpose**, not only for **Fundamental Rights**, so an ordinary legal right is also protected.

questions.stem_md: Who appoints a District Judge?

options.text_md: The President of India
The Governor of the State, in consultation with the High Court
The Chief Justice of India
The District Collector

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Governor of the State, in consultation with the High Court. Under Article 233, District Judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court of the State. The President appoints High Court judges, and a Collector is an executive officer.

questions.stem_md: An advocate who is not already in government service wishes to be appointed directly as a District Judge. For at least how many years must he have practised as an advocate?

options.text_md: Ten years
Three years
Fifteen years
Seven years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Seven years. Article 233 requires at least seven years as an advocate or pleader for direct appointment as a District Judge. Ten years is the requirement for a High Court judge.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined district, a man is charged with murder. Which court will try the case?

options.text_md: The Sessions Court
The Court of the District Judge sitting on a civil matter
A Lok Adalat
The High Court in its advisory jurisdiction

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Sessions Court. Serious criminal offences such as murder are tried by the Sessions Court. Civil matters go to the District Judge's court; Lok Adalats cannot settle serious non-compoundable crimes; High Courts have no advisory jurisdiction.

questions.stem_md: Why is the same judicial officer often described as both the District Judge and the Sessions Judge?

options.text_md: He is elected twice, once by lawyers and once by the people
He serves as District Judge in one State and Sessions Judge in another
He is called the District Judge when hearing civil cases and the Sessions Judge when hearing criminal cases
The titles are given by the Governor only during an emergency

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** He is called the District Judge when hearing civil cases and the Sessions Judge when hearing criminal cases. At the district level the senior-most judge usually handles both sides of the work: as District Judge for civil cases and as Sessions Judge for criminal cases. The other options describe arrangements that do not exist.

questions.stem_md: A Sessions Court in an imagined district sentences a convict to death. What must happen before the sentence can be carried out?

options.text_md: The District Collector must sign it
A Lok Adalat must approve it
The High Court must confirm the sentence
The State Assembly must pass a resolution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The High Court must confirm the sentence. A death sentence passed by a Sessions Court cannot be executed unless the High Court confirms it; the criminal procedure law requires this. Executive officers, Lok Adalats and legislatures have no such role.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a work of the Court of the District Judge?

options.text_md: Hearing appeals from lower civil courts in the district
Trying cases of murder and dacoity
Issuing writs to enforce Fundamental Rights
Electing members of the Rajya Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Hearing appeals from lower civil courts in the district. The District Judge's court hears civil appeals from lower civil courts of the district and also tries important civil suits. Serious crimes go to the Sessions Court; writs are issued by the High Court and Supreme Court.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The High Court is consulted before a District Judge is appointed.

**Reason (R):** The High Court supervises the subordinate courts of the State and is best placed to judge the fitness of judicial officers.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both statements are true, and R explains A. Because the High Court superintends the district judiciary, the Constitution requires the Governor to consult it on appointments, which also protects the independence of the lower courts.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Sessions Court mainly hears disputes about property, contracts and rent.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Property, contract and rent disputes are civil matters for civil courts headed by the District Judge. The Sessions Court tries serious criminal cases.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the courts in the order in which an imagined criminal case may climb, from where a serious offence is tried to the highest court of appeal.

options.text_md: Sessions Court (trial of the serious offence)
Supreme Court (further appeal)
High Court (appeal against the conviction)

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (a) → (c) → (b). A serious offence is tried by the Sessions Court; an appeal against conviction lies to the High Court; a further appeal may go to the Supreme Court.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State two functions of the Court of the District Judge.
questions.solution_md: Any two valid functions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It hears **appeals** against the decisions of **lower civil courts** in the district.
2. It tries important **civil suits** (for example about property or succession) and **supervises** the subordinate civil courts of the district.

questions.stem_md: State two functions of the Sessions Court.
questions.solution_md: Trials of serious crimes; appeals from magistrates.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It tries **serious criminal cases** such as murder, robbery and dacoity, and can pass any sentence allowed by law, including **death** (which needs **High Court confirmation**).
2. It hears **appeals** against judgements of **magistrates' courts** in the district.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the Court of the District Judge and the Sessions Court.
questions.solution_md: Civil versus criminal, with one example each.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Court of the District Judge** deals with **civil** cases: disputes about property, contracts, family matters and civil appeals. The **Sessions Court** deals with **criminal** cases: serious offences and appeals from magistrates.

questions.stem_md: Kavita (imagined) loses a dispute about her shop's rent in a lower civil court of her district. Trace three steps she could take through the courts if she remains dissatisfied.
questions.solution_md: District Judge, High Court, Supreme Court in order.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. She can appeal to the **Court of the District Judge**, which hears civil appeals from lower civil courts.
2. If she loses there, she can take a further appeal to the **High Court** of the State.
3. If a substantial question of law is involved, an appeal may finally lie to the **Supreme Court**. (At any stage the parties may also try to settle at a **Lok Adalat**.)

questions.stem_md:
Read the situation and answer. *(Imagined.)* A class visits the district court complex of Kesarganj and sees two courtrooms marked "District Judge" and "Sessions Judge".

(i) Explain how a District Judge is appointed and the qualification for direct appointment. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the functions of the Court of the District Judge. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the functions of the Sessions Court and explain why the same officer may sit in both courtrooms. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Appointment and qualification; civil functions; criminal functions and the dual title.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A District Judge is appointed by the **Governor** of the State **in consultation with the High Court** (**Article 233**). A person not already in judicial service must have been an **advocate for at least seven years** and be recommended by the High Court.

(ii) The Court of the District Judge is the **highest civil court** of the district. It hears **appeals** from lower civil courts, tries important **civil suits** about property, succession and contracts, and **supervises** the subordinate civil courts.

(iii) The **Sessions Court** tries **serious criminal cases** such as murder and dacoity, hears **appeals from magistrates**, and can pass any lawful sentence; a **death sentence** must be **confirmed by the High Court**. The **same judicial officer** usually heads both: he is called the **District Judge** when hearing **civil** matters and the **Sessions Judge** when hearing **criminal** matters.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Governor in consultation with the High Court
(iii) Same officer: District Judge and Sessions Judge

Study the hierarchy of courts in a State shown in the diagram and answer.

(i) Name the courts at each level from the district to the State, and say which kind of case each district court handles. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the High Court controls the courts below it. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate two advantages of having a single integrated hierarchy of courts in India. **[4]**

assets.caption: Hierarchy of courts in a State (schematic).

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) At the bottom are **lower civil courts** and **magistrates' courts**; above them, the **Court of the District Judge** (civil cases) and the **Sessions Court** (serious criminal cases); at the top of the State is the **High Court**, and above it the **Supreme Court**.

(ii) The High Court has **superintendence** over all courts and tribunals in its territory under **Article 227**; it hears **appeals** and **revisions** from them; it is **consulted** on the appointment, posting and promotion of district judges; and its judgements as a **Court of Record** bind them.

(iii) First, a **single chain of appeal** lets a citizen take a case from the district to the **Supreme Court**, so mistakes can be corrected. Second, decisions of higher courts **bind** lower courts, which keeps the **law uniform** across the country. A balanced view: the hierarchy also brings **delays**, which is why **Lok Adalats** are used to settle simpler disputes.

questions.stem_md: What is a Lok Adalat?

options.text_md: A special bench of the Supreme Court for constitutional cases
A village council that elects the sarpanch
A tribunal that hears appeals from the High Court
A people's court that settles disputes by compromise and agreement between the parties

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A people's court that settles disputes by compromise and agreement between the parties. A Lok Adalat ("people's court") settles pending or pre-litigation disputes by conciliation and mutual agreement. It is not a bench of the Supreme Court, an electoral body or an appeal tribunal.

questions.stem_md: Which law gave Lok Adalats statutory status?

options.text_md: The Representation of the People Act, 1951
The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
The Indian Councils Act, 1861
The Right to Information Act, 2005

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 gave Lok Adalats a statutory basis and made their awards binding. The other Acts deal with elections, colonial councils and access to information.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined neighbours settle a boundary dispute at a Lok Adalat. One of them later wants to appeal against the award. What is the position?

options.text_md: No appeal lies; the award is final and binding like a decree of a civil court
He may appeal to the High Court within one week
He may appeal to the Sessions Court
He may ask the Governor to cancel the award

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** No appeal lies; the award is final and binding like a decree of a civil court. An award of a Lok Adalat is treated as a decree of a civil court, is final and binding on the parties, and no appeal lies against it, because it is based on their own agreement.

questions.stem_md: A widow in an imagined town has a pending claim for insurance money and very little cash. Why might her lawyer suggest taking the case to a Lok Adalat?

options.text_md: A Lok Adalat can award her punishment against the insurer
No court fee is charged, and any fee already paid on a pending case is refunded if it is settled there
A Lok Adalat case automatically goes to the Supreme Court
Only lawyers above ten years' standing can appear there

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** No court fee is charged, and any fee already paid on a pending case is refunded if it is settled there. There is no court fee in a Lok Adalat, and the fee paid on a case pending in a regular court is refunded when the case is settled there, so it suits a person of small means. A Lok Adalat does not punish, does not send cases to the Supreme Court, and is informal.

questions.stem_md: Which of these disputes is a Lok Adalat NOT meant to settle?

options.text_md: A claim for compensation after a road accident
A dispute between a bank and a borrower over a loan
A serious criminal charge, such as murder, that the law does not allow to be compromised
A quarrel between neighbours over a drain

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A serious criminal charge, such as murder, that the law does not allow to be compromised. Lok Adalats settle civil disputes and compoundable matters by agreement; offences that the law does not allow to be compromised, such as murder, must be tried by the regular criminal courts. Accident claims, bank loans and neighbourhood quarrels are typical Lok Adalat matters.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lok Adalats help reduce the number of cases pending in regular courts.

**Reason (R):** They settle disputes quickly through informal procedure and agreement, without the long stages of a regular trial.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both statements are true, and R explains A. Because cases are settled by compromise in a single sitting or a few sittings, many disputes leave the regular courts, easing the backlog.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An award made by a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, a Lok Adalat's award is deemed a decree of a civil court and is final and binding.

questions.stem_md: The words "Lok Adalat" mean a ___ court.
questions.solution_md: Lok Adalat means a people's court.

questions.stem_md: Give two advantages of Lok Adalats for ordinary citizens.
questions.solution_md: Any two valid advantages.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Justice is **quick and cheap**: **no court fee** is charged, and fee paid on a pending case is **refunded** on settlement.
2. The procedure is **informal** and based on **agreement**, so the parties stay on good terms and **no appeal** drags it on.

questions.stem_md: Who usually conducts a Lok Adalat, and what kinds of cases can come before it?
questions.solution_md: Who presides; what cases.

answer.model_answer_md: A Lok Adalat is usually conducted by a **serving or retired judicial officer** with **one or two other members**, such as a lawyer or social worker. Cases can be **pending in a court** or **at the pre-litigation stage**, mainly **civil** and **compoundable** disputes.

questions.stem_md: Compare a Lok Adalat with a regular civil court on three points.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct points of comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Method:** a Lok Adalat settles by **compromise**; a regular court **decides** after a contested trial.
2. **Cost and speed:** a Lok Adalat charges **no court fee** and is **quick**; a regular court involves **fees** and often **long delays**.
3. **Appeal:** a Lok Adalat's award is **final, with no appeal**; a regular court's decree can be **appealed** to a higher court.

questions.stem_md:
Read the situation and answer. *(Imagined.)* A district in Varunpradesh has tens of thousands of cases waiting in its courts, many of them over small loans, rent and road accidents.

(i) Explain what a Lok Adalat is and how it works. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the legal status of its awards. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate how far Lok Adalats can help this district, giving one limitation. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning and working; legal status; evaluation with a limitation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A **Lok Adalat** is a **people's court** where a **judicial officer** with one or two other members helps the parties reach a **compromise**. It takes up cases **pending in courts** or at the **pre-litigation** stage, works **informally** and charges **no court fee**.

(ii) Under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**, an award is **deemed a decree of a civil court**. It is **final and binding** on the parties and **no appeal** lies against it; fee paid on a pending case is **refunded**.

(iii) Lok Adalats suit this district well: loan, rent and accident claims are usually **civil and compoundable**, and **one sitting** can settle **many cases**, cutting the **backlog** and saving **money** for poor litigants. A **limitation** is that they work only when **both sides agree**; a party who refuses, or a **serious criminal** case, must still go to the regular courts.

questions.stem_md: A permanent judge of an imagined High Court falls ill for six months. Whom can the President appoint to do that judge's work meanwhile?

options.text_md: A Lok Adalat bench
The District Collector
A member of the State Legislative Council
An acting judge

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** An acting judge. When a permanent judge is absent or unable to act, the President may appoint an acting judge (Article 224). The other options are not judges of the High Court.

questions.stem_md: A citizen of an imagined State wants a writ against an officer working in that same State. Which statement about where she can go is correct?

options.text_md: She may approach only the Court of the District Judge
She may approach only a Lok Adalat
She must first obtain the Governor's permission
She may approach either the High Court of the State or, for a Fundamental Right, the Supreme Court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** She may approach either the High Court of the State or, for a Fundamental Right, the Supreme Court. A High Court can issue writs within its territory under Article 226, and the Supreme Court can issue writs for Fundamental Rights under Article 32, so she has a choice. District courts and Lok Adalats do not issue writs, and no permission is needed.

questions.stem_md: A convict is unhappy with a judgement of a Judicial Magistrate's court in a theft case. To which court does his first appeal normally go?

options.text_md: The Court of the District Judge on its civil side
The Supreme Court directly
The Sessions Court
A Lok Adalat

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Sessions Court. Appeals against judgements of magistrates in criminal cases go to the Sessions Court. Civil appeals go to the District Judge, the Supreme Court is not the first appeal court, and a Lok Adalat does not hear appeals.

questions.stem_md: Which of these best describes the members of a typical Lok Adalat bench?

options.text_md: Three elected members of the State Legislative Assembly
A serving or retired judicial officer, often joined by a lawyer or a social worker
The Governor and two ministers
Five judges of the Supreme Court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A serving or retired judicial officer, often joined by a lawyer or a social worker. A Lok Adalat bench is usually headed by a serving or retired judicial officer, with one or two other members such as a lawyer or social worker. Legislators, ministers and Supreme Court benches do not conduct Lok Adalats.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following can a High Court examine under its power of judicial review?

options.text_md: Both laws made by the State Legislature and laws made by Parliament, as well as executive orders
Only the orders of the District Collector
Only laws made before 1950
Only decisions of Lok Adalats

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both laws made by the State Legislature and laws made by Parliament, as well as executive orders. A High Court can test any law, State or Union, and any executive order against the Constitution and declare it void if it violates it. Its review is not limited to Collectors' orders, older laws or Lok Adalat awards.

questions.stem_md: A bank in an imagined town has hundreds of small unpaid loans. Explain why it might prefer a Lok Adalat to filing separate suits.
questions.solution_md: Speed, cost and finality for a large number of small cases.

answer.model_answer_md: Many loan cases can be **settled in one sitting** by **agreement** with borrowers, saving **time** and **court fees**; the **award is final**, so the bank recovers money **without long appeals**.
